w: What's tested Cryptorchidism (a testis that didn't come down): it raises the risk of infertility and testicular cancer Testicular tumors: almost all are germ cell tumors; seminoma versus everything else Infections: syphilis, gonorrhea and chlamydia of the penis; gonorrhea and chlamydia of the epididymis The prostate: BPH around the urethra blocks urine; cancer in the outer zone, found with PSA, spreads to bone, graded by Gleason HPV: types 6 and 11 cause benign warts; 16 and 18 cause precancer The bladder: urothelial carcinoma, and smoking Dr. Dal Zotto, a pathologist, covered the bladder and then the male organs: the penis, the testis and the prostate. These notes follow the recording. The urinary tract Urine flows from the kidney's pelvis down the two ureters to the bladder and out the urethra. All of it is lined by the urothelium, a tough lining of 5 to 7 cell layers with big umbrella cells on top, because urine is toxic. Only the very end of the urethra has skin-like squamous lining. Benign bladder problems Babies can be born with a double ureter, or with reflux, where urine flows back up toward the kidney and causes repeated infections. In exstrophy, the belly wall doesn't close and the bladder is exposed. Kidney stones get stuck where the ureter is narrow, especially where it enters the bladder. Cystitis, a bladder infection, comes from skin bacteria moving up the urethra. A diverticulum is a pouch pushed out through a weak spot in the bladder wall; it can get infected and later turn into cancer. Bladder cancer It's the fourth most common cancer in men and rare in women. Most urinary tract tumors, 90 percent, are urothelial carcinomas, and most are in the bladder. The main sign is a little blood in the urine, with no pain for years. Smoking is the big risk factor: four times the risk, and quitting doesn't bring it down. Dyes, rubber and leather work, pelvic radiation, cyclophosphamide and chronic catheters add risk, and a parasite, Schistosoma, causes squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder in Egypt. It isn't very deadly, but it's expensive, because patients are watched for life. The deeper it grows into the bladder wall, the worse the outlook. The penis In hypospadias the urethra opens on the underside; in epispadias, on top. In phimosis the foreskin is too tight to pull back. Dirt and dead cells build up under it, cause inflammation, and over years can lead to cancer of the penis. Infections include syphilis, gonorrhea and chlamydia. HPV and the penis Genital warts (condyloma acuminatum) are benign and come from HPV types 6 and 11, the low numbers. Precancer (penile intraepithelial neoplasia) comes from types 16 and 18, the high numbers, and looks flat and red, not warty. Untreated, about 30 percent become invasive cancer. Older men can get a precancer without HPV, from chronic inflammation and lichen sclerosus. Penile cancer is rare in the United States, grows slowly and spreads to the groin's lymph nodes. The testis The testis sits in the scrotum because making sperm needs a cooler place than the body. Inside are tubules where sperm cells mature, guided by Sertoli cells; Leydig cells between the tubules make testosterone. A hydrocele is fluid around the testis. Epididymitis is often from gonorrhea or chlamydia. Orchitis, an infection of the testis itself, is rare. Two emergencies: torsion, where the testis twists and loses its blood supply, and an inguinal hernia, where a loop of bowel gets trapped in the groin. Cryptorchidism The testes start inside the body and move down into the scrotum before birth. If one stays hidden (crypto means hidden), doctors wait a year or two, then fix it with surgery by about age 2. Body heat stops sperm from being made, so it can cause infertility and testicular cancer. Surgery prevents the infertility, but the cancer risk stays. Testicular tumors 95 percent are germ cell tumors, from the cells that make sperm. The split to know is seminoma versus non-seminoma. Seminoma is the most common: a white, solid tumor in men in their 30s and 40s, with no blood test marker, and it responds to radiation. The others (embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, teratoma) are more aggressive and don't respond as well. Even so, more than 95 percent of germ cell tumors are cured. The prostate BPH, a benign growth around the urethra, comes to almost every man after 50 and makes it hard to urinate; severe cases get surgery. Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men, usually after 65. It starts in the outer zone, so it doesn't block urine early. A blood test, PSA, finds it. It spreads to bone and makes extra bone. The Gleason grade says how abnormal the glands look: the less they look like normal glands, the worse the outlook.
